title: CooperTrim: Adaptive Data Selection for Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Perception
one_liner: When robots share sensor data to help each other see, pick only the features that capture what is changing right now, not what stayed the same, so you send less data without losing accuracy.
lead: Autonomous robots see better when they radio each other what they observe, because each robot fills in blind spots the other robot has—what one robot's camera sees, its partner's camera might miss. But wireless bandwidth is limited, so sending all sensor data is too expensive. CooperTrim exploits a simple fact: most of the features in a sensor frame are static (trees, roads, buildings do not move much), while a few features change from moment to moment (pedestrians, cars, obstacles). By measuring which features are changing and skipping the static ones, CooperTrim cuts bandwidth by over 80 percent while keeping accuracy the same.

problem.h2: Wireless bandwidth chokes on sensor data
paras: When an autonomous car or robot shares its sensor view with nearby robots, it sends dense encoded representations (lists of numbers from cameras and lidar) over radio. Wireless links have fixed bandwidth—there is only so much data per second you can push through the air.

A naive approach sends every feature from every sensor frame. This works if bandwidth is free, but real wireless networks are constrained. The alternatives try to compress (lose some detail) or select a subset of features (keep the most important ones). But even with selection, if you pick the same features every frame, you end up sending a lot of redundant static information—the same building edges, road markings, sky pixels over and over, because they do not change.

The fundamental problem: existing selection methods do not account for time. They treat each frame independently and pick the same important-looking features frame after frame. They cannot tell the difference between a feature that is important because it is always prominent (a building, a road edge, something that stayed the same across 100 frames) and a feature that is important because it just changed (a pedestrian entered the frame, a car moved into view). Static things and moving things both look important to a model that only sees one frame.

callout.html: Pick only the features that are changing, not the ones that stayed the same, and transmit them selectively based on how much the scene is moving.

panels.title: 1. Robot sees via sensors
panels.caption: Camera and lidar encode 500 features per frame; all are packed into one radio message.

panels.title: 2. The bandwidth wall
panels.viz_args: Wireless link: 50 kilobits/sec. Message: 400 kilobits. Mismatch.
panels.caption: Sending everything takes 8 seconds; robots need answers in 0.1 seconds.

panels.title: 3. Most features do not move
panels.caption: Buildings, roads: same every frame. Pedestrians, cars: new each frame.

panels.title: 4. Measure temporal change
panels.viz_args: Uncertainty score per feature: how much does it vary frame to frame?
panels.caption: High uncertainty, send it. Low uncertainty, skip it. Adaptive per frame.

panels.title: 5. Bandwidth drops, accuracy holds
panels.caption: 80% smaller message. Robot partner still sees moving objects correctly.

steps.text: Sensor feeds (camera, lidar) produce a list of 500+ numerical features via a neural network encoder.
For each feature, compute a confidence score: how much does this feature vary across the last few frames? Features that stay flat have low confidence; features that jump around have high confidence.

Use the past features as a reference. A cross-attention mechanism (a learned comparison between two sets of features) ranks current features by how well they predict the segmentation task. Assign each feature a relevance score: does it matter to the segmentation task right now?

Decide a cutoff based on the scene complexity: in a simple static scene, use a low threshold (send few features); in a busy intersection with moving objects, use a high threshold (send more). Create a binary mask.
Send only the unmasked features over radio. The receiving robot fuses them with its own features to make a joint map.

paras: The paper changes which features get transmitted per frame. Instead of selecting a fixed set of features (the same ones every frame), CooperTrim computes a dynamic mask: a set of on-off switches that change per frame based on temporal uncertainty (how much each feature is moving) and task relevance.

hidden.name: Temporal uncertainty
paras: Temporal uncertainty is a number (from 0 to 1) that measures how much a single feature varies across consecutive frames. A static feature (road edge) has low temporal uncertainty. A changing feature (new pedestrian) has high uncertainty.

The paper estimates this using a learned model. The model takes the current frame and the previous frame and outputs a confidence score for each feature—how confident is the model that this feature will change in the next frame? High confidence means high uncertainty, so transmit it. Low confidence means low uncertainty, so skip it.

heat.caption: Darker means higher temporal uncertainty (feature varies more). Highlight means will be transmitted.

reads.html: Static things (buildings, sidewalks) have low temporal uncertainty. Moving things (pedestrians, cars) have high temporal uncertainty.
Temporal uncertainty is estimated via conformal prediction inspired quantile gating. A learned quantile threshold q separates low-variance features (keep low) from high-variance features (transmit).

paras: When transmitting a live map to a teammate over a low-bandwidth radio link, every byte counts. The world updates frame to frame. Some things stay the same (buildings, roads); some things change (people move, cars drive). If you send the full feature set every time, you waste bandwidth re-transmitting the static parts. But if you send only what changed, your teammate's map updates cleanly without redundancy.

CooperTrim measures temporal uncertainty for each feature: Does this feature look different this frame than last frame? If yes, transmit it. If no, skip it. The catch: a feature might be important for the overall task (segmentation accuracy) but unchanging (road edges are stable but critical for safe navigation). CooperTrim uses a second signal, cross-attention (a learned comparison between current and historical features), to catch these. It learns which stable features are task-critical and which are noise. A feature that is stable AND task-critical still gets sent, but a feature that is stable AND low-relevance gets dropped.

Finally, the transmission threshold adapts to scene complexity. In a simple, static scene (a parked car in an empty lot), the model sets a high bar for transmission: send almost nothing, because almost nothing changes. In a busy intersection, the model lowers the bar: send more, because more is changing. This adaptation is learned during training via a reinforcement-learning inspired strategy that balances using all data (expensive, uses full bandwidth) versus partial data (risky, misses information) to find the optimal transmission set.

stages.s: Current frame (500 features) and previous frame (500 features)
Compute temporal uncertainty for each feature
Cross-attention: rank by relevance to task
Adaptive threshold: set cutoff based on scene complexity

math.words: Total loss is task performance plus a penalty term that controls bandwidth usage. Transmission of a feature f at time t is selected if temporal uncertainty score is above a learned quantile threshold q, weighted by relevance score R from cross-attention, and summed against a dynamic transmission target C that adapts per frame.
symbols: segmentation accuracy loss given selected features C
penalty weight, learned during training to balance accuracy vs bandwidth
total bytes transmitted for the selected feature set
target bandwidth budget per frame (e.g., 1.6 kilobits)
the set of selected features (binary mask)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 10 features. Current frame: task loss L_task = 0.05 (low error, good accuracy). Transmitted bytes P = 40 bytes. Target C_target = 25 bytes.
Lambda is set to 10 (fairly high penalty for over-transmission). Constraint violation = 40 - 25 = 15 bytes over.
Total loss = 0.05 + 10 * 15 = 150.05. Training sees this high penalty and learns to drop low-uncertainty features next iteration.

Next frame, 6 features are selected (new mask). P = 18 bytes (under budget). Loss = 0.08 (slightly worse accuracy, because we dropped some useful features) + 10 * (18 - 25) = 0.08 - 70 = nearly zero. Penalty term is negative (reward for staying under budget).
Training finds a balance: select features so that P hovers near C_target, keeping accuracy loss small.

math.note: The total loss pulls in two directions: high task performance (send more features) and low bandwidth (send fewer features). Lambda adjusts the strength of each pull. The model learns which features earn their transmission cost.

charts.title: Naive: send all features
charts.note: Full feature set keeps accuracy high but chokes wireless links and introduces transmission delay.

charts.title: CooperTrim: adaptive selection
charts.note: Selecting only changing + relevant features cuts bandwidth by 81% and latency by 85%, with only 3% accuracy drop.

items.html: If a busy intersection appears without warning (e.g., at a road turn), the temporal uncertainty model may not have seen similar complexity before. In the first few frames, it will still transmit few features. The segmentation will fail until the model catches up. A solution: use a conservative preset for uncertain situations (traffic lights, intersections) learned offline.

items.b: Static but critical features get dropped.
items.html: A road edge or lane marker is stable across frames but essential for safe navigation. Temporal uncertainty alone will drop it. CooperTrim uses task relevance (cross-attention) to catch these, but if the attention model is poorly trained, critical static features may be missed.

items.b: Bandwidth target is set too low.
items.html: If C_target is smaller than the minimum viable feature set for the task, no training will recover. The segmentation will fail even on simple scenes. The paper sets C_target via offline calibration (find the threshold where accuracy drops noticeably).

The paper empirically validates that the model learns to adapt: in simple scenes it sends ~50 features; in complex scenes it sends ~150 features. Qualitative results show the model gracefully scales transmission with environmental complexity.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement CooperTrim on a two-robot cooperative segmentation setup: Robot A encodes a lidar/camera frame, computes temporal uncertainty for each feature, ranks by cross-attention relevance, applies the adaptive mask, and sends selected features over a simulated low-bandwidth channel (e.g., 100 kilobits per second) to Robot B. Robot B fuses the sparse features with its own observations to produce a joint segmentation map (a 2D label grid of road, pedestrian, car, etc.). Run this on a real dataset like nuScenes (urban driving scenes with multi-agent annotations) for 100 consecutive frames.
demo.metric_eq: Segmentation IoU = (pixels correctly labeled AND selected) / (pixels correctly labeled OR selected) over all frames; Bandwidth = total bytes sent / total possible bytes; Efficiency gain = (IoU_naive - IoU_trim) / (Bandwidth_naive - Bandwidth_trim), should be negative (IoU barely drops while bandwidth drops sharply).
demo.closing: The demo should make visible that CooperTrim transmits a flurry of features during complex motion (e.g., multiple pedestrians crossing) and goes silent during static scenes (e.g., parked cars), proving that temporal uncertainty adapts transmission to what is actually changing.
